questions.prompt: What is overfitting?
options: The model fits noise in the training data and performs poorly on unseen data
The model is too simple to capture the pattern in the data
The model trains too slowly to finish
The model is trained on too few features
questions.explanation: An overfit model memorises training specifics instead of learning patterns that generalise.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an example of supervised learning?
options: Grouping customers by behaviour with no labels
Predicting house prices from past sales with known sale prices
Reducing images to two dimensions with PCA
Discovering topics in unlabelled documents
questions.explanation: Supervised learning uses labelled examples (here, known prices) to learn a mapping from inputs to outputs.

questions.prompt: Why do we hold out a test set that is not used during training?
options: To make training run faster
To increase the amount of training data
To tune the learning rate automatically
To estimate how well the model generalises to unseen data
questions.explanation: Performance on training data is optimistic; held-out data gives an unbiased estimate.

questions.prompt: Which is a standard metric for evaluating a regression model?
options: Precision
F1 score
Mean squared error
Confusion matrix
questions.explanation: MSE measures the average squared difference between predictions and true numeric targets.

questions.prompt: In gradient descent, what does the learning rate control?
options: The size of each parameter update step
The number of features used
The number of training examples per epoch
The number of layers in the model
questions.explanation: Too large a rate can overshoot the minimum; too small makes learning slow.

questions.prompt: In machine learning, what is a feature?
options: The value the model is trying to predict
An input variable used by the model to make predictions
A hyperparameter set before training
A metric for model quality
questions.explanation: Features are the measurable inputs; the thing being predicted is the label or target.

questions.prompt: Logistic regression is mainly used for what kind of task?
options: Predicting unbounded continuous values
Clustering unlabelled data
Classification, by predicting class probabilities
Dimensionality reduction
questions.explanation: Despite its name, logistic regression models the probability of class membership.

questions.prompt: A dataset is 99% negative and 1% positive. Why is accuracy a poor metric here?
options: Accuracy cannot be computed for imbalanced data
Accuracy only works for regression
A model that always predicts negative scores 99% accuracy while finding no positives
Accuracy ignores the negative class
questions.explanation: Accuracy is dominated by the majority class, so metrics such as recall, precision or PR-AUC are more informative.

questions.prompt: Which practice causes data leakage?
options: Fitting a feature scaler on the full dataset before splitting into train and test
Fitting the scaler on the training data only
Splitting data before any preprocessing
Using a pipeline that fits transforms on training folds only
questions.explanation: Test-set statistics leak into training, producing over-optimistic evaluation results.

questions.prompt: Compared with L2 regularisation, what is a typical effect of L1 regularisation?
options: It never changes the weights
It only increases weights
It removes the need for a validation set
It tends to drive some weights exactly to zero, giving sparse models
questions.explanation: The L1 penalty has a sharp corner at zero that encourages sparsity, whereas L2 shrinks weights smoothly.

questions.prompt: Training accuracy is 99% and validation accuracy is 70%. Which next step is most appropriate?
options: Add more layers to the model
Add regularisation or collect more training data
Train for many more epochs
Remove the validation set
questions.explanation: A large train-validation gap indicates overfitting, which regularisation or more data helps to reduce.

questions.prompt: What is the main purpose of k-fold cross-validation?
options: To get a more reliable performance estimate by averaging over several train-validation splits
To make the model train in parallel
To increase the amount of labelled data
To remove the need for a final test set
questions.explanation: Each example is used for validation exactly once, reducing the variance of the estimate.

questions.prompt: How is precision defined?
options: True positives divided by all actual positives
True negatives divided by all predicted negatives
Correct predictions divided by all predictions
True positives divided by all predicted positives
questions.explanation: Precision = TP / (TP + FP); the version dividing by actual positives is recall.

questions.prompt: Which algorithm is most sensitive to features being on very different scales?
options: Decision tree
k-nearest neighbours
Random forest
Gradient-boosted trees
questions.explanation: k-NN relies on distances, so large-scale features dominate; tree methods split on single-feature thresholds.

questions.prompt: How does increasing k in k-nearest neighbours typically change the bias-variance trade-off?
options: Bias decreases and variance increases
Bias increases and variance decreases
Both bias and variance decrease
Both bias and variance increase
questions.explanation: Larger k smooths the decision boundary, which is less flexible but less sensitive to individual points.

questions.prompt: Why do deep networks with sigmoid activations tend to suffer from vanishing gradients?
options: The sigmoid output is always negative
Sigmoid makes the loss function non-differentiable
The sigmoid derivative is at most 0.25 and saturates, so repeated multiplication shrinks gradients
Sigmoid doubles the weights at every layer
questions.explanation: Backpropagation multiplies many small derivative terms, so gradients in early layers become tiny.

questions.prompt: Why is PR-AUC often more informative than ROC-AUC under heavy class imbalance?
options: ROC's false positive rate is dominated by the huge negative class, hiding many false positives
ROC-AUC cannot be computed with imbalanced classes
PR-AUC ignores the positive class
PR curves do not depend on the threshold
questions.explanation: Precision directly reflects false positives relative to predicted positives, so it exposes poor performance on the rare class.

questions.prompt: Beyond bootstrap sampling, what reduces correlation between trees in a random forest?
options: Each tree is trained on a different loss function
Trees are pruned to depth one
Each tree uses the previous tree's residuals
Each split considers only a random subset of features
questions.explanation: Random feature subsets prevent all trees from choosing the same dominant splits, so averaging reduces variance more.

questions.prompt: During inference, which statistics does batch normalisation use?
options: Running mean and variance accumulated during training
The mean and variance of the current test batch
Zero mean and unit variance fixed at initialisation
The statistics of the validation loss
questions.explanation: Using stored running estimates makes predictions deterministic and independent of the batch composition.

questions.prompt: In gradient boosting, what does each new tree fit?
options: A fresh bootstrap sample of the labels
The average of all previous trees' predictions
The negative gradient of the loss with respect to the current ensemble's predictions
Only the examples that were misclassified, with the other examples removed
questions.explanation: For squared error this is simply the residuals; each tree takes a gradient-descent step in function space.

questions.prompt: Why is randomly shuffled k-fold cross-validation usually inappropriate for time-series forecasting?
options: Time series cannot be split into folds
It uses too little data for validation
It makes the model underfit
Training folds can contain observations later than the validation points, leaking future information
questions.explanation: Forecast evaluation must respect time order, for example with expanding-window or rolling-origin splits.
